claim: Global food security will be challenged by the effect of climate change on crop yields in the near future.
source: In the near future, global food security will be challenged by the effect of climate change on crop yields (Schwalm et al., 2017; Tirado et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schwalm et al., 2017 and Tirado et al., 2013

claim: Anhydrobiotes include bacteria, yeast, plant seeds, resurrection ferns, tardigrades and nematodes.
source: Anhydrobiotes include single celled organisms (bacteria and yeast), simple multicellular organisms (plant seeds), as well as complex multicellular plants and animals (resurrection ferns, tardigrades and nematodes).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about anhydrobiotes

claim: Almost all anhydrobiotes have high levels of the disaccharide trehalose and small, hydrophilic, and intrinsically disordered proteins collectively called hydrophilins.
source: An important clue to the identification of critical stress effectors of desiccation came from the discovery that almost all anhydrobiotes have high levels of the disaccharide trehalose and small, hydrophilic, and intrinsically disordered proteins collectively called hydrophilins (Crowe et al., 1992; Potts, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crowe et al., 1992 and Potts, 2001

claim: Nematodes lacking trehalose are extremely sensitive to short term desiccation.
source: Nematodes lacking trehalose are extremely sensitive to short term desiccation, while yeast lacking trehalose are sensitive to only long term-tolerance desiccation (Erkut et al., 2011; Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkut et al., 2011 and Tapia and Koshland, 2014

claim: Yeast lacking trehalose are sensitive to only long term-tolerance desiccation.
source: Nematodes lacking trehalose are extremely sensitive to short term desiccation, while yeast lacking trehalose are sensitive to only long term-tolerance desiccation (Erkut et al., 2011; Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkut et al., 2011 and Tapia and Koshland, 2014

claim: At least one species of tardigrade is desiccation tolerant although naturally lacking trehalose.
source: At least one species of tardigrade is desiccation tolerant although naturally lacking trehalose (Boothby et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Boothby et al., 2017

claim: Only 0.001% of exponentially dividing yeast cells survive desiccation compared to 20–40% survival of stationary phase cells.
source: Only 0.001% of exponentially dividing yeast cells survive desiccation compared to 20–40% survival of stationary phase cells (Calahan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calahan et al., 2011

claim: After drying, desiccation sensitive nematodes exhibit membrane blebbing.
source: After drying, desiccation sensitive nematodes and yeast exhibit membrane blebbing and protein aggregation, respectively (Erkut et al., 2011; Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkut et al., 2011 and Tapia and Koshland, 2014

claim: After drying, desiccation sensitive yeast exhibit protein aggregation.
source: After drying, desiccation sensitive nematodes and yeast exhibit membrane blebbing and protein aggregation, respectively (Erkut et al., 2011; Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Erkut et al., 2011 and Tapia and Koshland, 2014

claim: Trehalose and Hsp12 synergize to completely alleviate all of the lethal damage that occurs due to severe water loss.
source: Here, using genetic assays with stationary and exponential phase cells, we demonstrate that trehalose and a single hydrophilin, Hsp12, unexpectedly synergize to completely alleviate all of the lethal damage that occurs due to severe water loss.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from genetic assays described in the manuscript

claim: Hsp12 encodes one of 12 previously identified yeast hydrophilins.
source: Hsp12 encodes one of 12 previously identified yeast hydrophilins and is the most highly expressed member of the family in stationary phase cells (Garay-Arroyo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garay-Arroyo et al., 2000

claim: Hsp12 is the most highly expressed hydrophilin in stationary phase cells.
source: Hsp12 encodes one of 12 previously identified yeast hydrophilins and is the most highly expressed member of the family in stationary phase cells (Garay-Arroyo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garay-Arroyo et al., 2000

claim: After a 30 day desiccation period, the viability of stationary phase wild type cells decreased only two-fold.
source: After a 30 day desiccation period, the viability of stationary phase wild type cells decreased only two-fold (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: After the 30 day desiccation period, tps1∆ cell viability dropped more than 100-fold.
source: Although the viability of tps1∆ cells was similar to that of wild type cells after two days of desiccation, after the 30 day desiccation period, tps1∆ cell viability dropped more than 100-fold (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: hsp12∆ cells exhibited wild type levels of desiccation tolerance after both short- and long-term desiccation.
source: While hsp12∆ cells exhibited wild type levels of desiccation tolerance after both short- and long-term desiccation, the tps1∆hsp12∆ cells displayed a 100-fold drop in viability after only 2 days of drying.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from desiccation tolerance assays

claim: tps1∆hsp12∆ cells displayed a 100-fold drop in viability after only 2 days of drying.
source: While hsp12∆ cells exhibited wild type levels of desiccation tolerance after both short- and long-term desiccation, the tps1∆hsp12∆ cells displayed a 100-fold drop in viability after only 2 days of drying.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from desiccation tolerance assays

claim: After 30 days of desiccation, no viable tps1∆hsp12∆ cells remained.
source: Furthermore, after 30 days of desiccation, no viable tps1∆hsp12∆ cells remained (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A

claim: The tps1∆hsp12∆ double mutant was no more heat-sensitive than either single mutant alone.
source: Furthermore, although tps1∆ and hsp12∆ had both been shown to confer elevated sensitivity to heat stress, the tps1∆hsp12∆ double mutant was no more heat-sensitive than either single mutant alone (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Gibney et al., 2015; Welker et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and citations to Gibney et al., 2015 and Welker et al., 2010

claim: The protective synergism between trehalose and Hsp12 is specific to desiccation stress.
source: Thus, the protective synergism we observe between trehalose and Hsp12 is specific to desiccation stress.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that the double mutant shows no additional heat sensitivity compared to single mutants

claim: Exponentially dividing cells with engineered high-level expression of Hsp12 exhibited a 1000-fold increase in desiccation tolerance.
source: These dividing cells exhibited a 1000-fold increase in desiccation tolerance, comparable to survival conferred by increased intracellular trehalose (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: The desiccation tolerance of exponentially-dividing yeast cells containing high levels of both trehalose and Hsp12 was ~60 fold greater than cells that expressed only Hsp12 or trehalose.
source: The desiccation tolerance of these cells was ~60 fold greater than cells that expressed only Hsp12 or trehalose.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from desiccation tolerance assays

claim: The absolute amount of tolerance (65–80% survival) of exponentially-dividing cells with both trehalose and Hsp12 was even greater than the tolerance of wild type cells in stationary phase (20–40% survival).
source: Furthermore, the absolute amount of tolerance (65–80% survival) was even greater than the tolerance of wild type cells in stationary phase (20–40% survival), the highest tolerance previously reported for yeast cells (Figure 1B) (Calahan et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Calahan et al., 2011

claim: Desiccation of CS caused an approximately 50% reduction in its enzymatic activity.
source: Desiccation of CS caused an approximately 50% reduction in its enzymatic activity (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: The presence of Hsp12 during drying maintained nearly all CS enzymatic activity in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: The presence of Hsp12 during drying maintained nearly all CS enzymatic activity in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Hsp12 on its own can stabilize protein activity against desiccation in vitro.
source: These results suggest that Hsp12 on its own can stabilize protein activity against desiccation in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the CS enzymatic activity data

claim: When dried alone, CS demonstrated high levels of aggregation, a 20-fold increase in its aggregation.
source: When dried alone, CS demonstrated high levels of aggregation, a 20-fold increase in its aggregation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Increasing amounts of Hsp12 added before desiccation decreased aggregation of CS in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Increasing amounts of Hsp12 added before desiccation decreased aggregation of CS in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Significant solubilization of CS occurred at a 2:1 ratio of Hsp12 to CS.
source: Significant solubilization of CS occurred at a 2:1 ratio of Hsp12 to CS (Figure 2B, 225:120 µg/ml).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: The stoichiometry of Hsp12 to CS suggests this solubilization function of Hsp12 is not enzymatic.
source: This stoichiometry suggests this solubilization function of Hsp12 is not enzymatic, consistent with Hsp12s high expression during stress in vivo.
evidence: Inferred from the 2:1 stoichiometry observed

claim: Increased Hsp12 expression significantly increased luciferase solubility after desiccation.
source: Increased Hsp12 expression significantly increased luciferase solubility.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from luciferase solubility assays

claim: Both in vivo and in vitro, Hsp12 helps mitigate desiccation-induced protein aggregation.
source: Thus, both in vivo and in vitro, Hsp12 helps mitigate desiccation-induced protein aggregation.
evidence: Inferred from the CS and FFL aggregation data

claim: Trehalose increased the activity and solubility of CS after desiccation in a concentration dependent manner.
source: In vitro, trehalose, like Hsp12, increased the activity and solubility of CS after desiccation in a concentration dependent manner (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F (note: these panel labels appear to be incorrect in the text as the figure only shows panels A-D)

claim: In vivo FFL activity was stabilized four-fold against desiccation in cells with high trehalose alone, but 14-fold in cells with both high Hsp12 and trehalose.
source: In vivo FFL activity was stabilized four-fold against desiccation in cells with high trehalose alone, but 14-fold in cells with both high Hsp12 and trehalose (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C (note: this panel label appears to be incorrect as Figure 2 shows panels A-D with different content)

claim: Hsp12 and trehalose can modulate the activity and solubility of proteins independently or cooperatively depending upon the substrates.
source: These results demonstrate that Hsp12 and trehalose can modulate the activity and solubility of proteins independently or cooperatively depending upon the substrates, suggesting that Hsp12 and trehalose have both independent and dependent functions in proteostasis.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects on CS and FFL

claim: [PSI+] is a cytoplasmic prion.
source: Previously, we showed that [PSI+], a cytoplasmic prion, or [GAR+], a membrane-associated prion, are propagated efficiently between desiccated stationary phase cells and their daughter cells that form upon rehydration in growth media (Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tapia and Koshland, 2014 and established knowledge

claim: [GAR+] is a membrane-associated prion.
source: Previously, we showed that [PSI+], a cytoplasmic prion, or [GAR+], a membrane-associated prion, are propagated efficiently between desiccated stationary phase cells and their daughter cells that form upon rehydration in growth media (Tapia and Koshland, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tapia and Koshland, 2014 and established knowledge

claim: hsp12∆ cells were able to propagate [PSI+] with or without desiccation.
source: Unlike tps1∆ cells, hsp12∆ cells were able to propagate [PSI+] with or without desiccation, suggesting that trehalose, but not Hsp12, is required to prevent [PSI+] hyper-aggregation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Trehalose, but not Hsp12, is required to prevent [PSI+] hyper-aggregation.
source: Unlike tps1∆ cells, hsp12∆ cells were able to propagate [PSI+] with or without desiccation, suggesting that trehalose, but not Hsp12, is required to prevent [PSI+] hyper-aggregation (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from the [PSI+] propagation data

claim: Even in the absence of desiccation, the percentage of [GAR+] cells in tps1∆hsp12∆ cultures was reduced almost 500-fold relative to wild type or hsp12∆ cells, and 50-fold relative to tps1∆.
source: Even in the absence of desiccation, the percentage of [GAR+] cells in tps1∆hsp12∆ cultures was reduced almost 500-fold relative to wild type or hsp12∆ cells, and 50-fold relative to tps1∆ (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Hsp12 and trehalose promote propagation of the membrane prion [GAR+] even under aqueous conditions.
source: Thus, Hsp12 and trehalose promote propagation of this membrane prion even under aqueous conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the [GAR+] propagation data in non-desiccated conditions

claim: After desiccation, the percentage of [GAR+] cells was unchanged in hsp12∆ mutant cells but was undetectable in both the tps1∆ and tps1∆hsp12∆ cells.
source: After desiccation, the percentage of [GAR+] cells was unchanged in hsp12∆ mutant cells but was undetectable in both the tps1∆ and tps1∆hsp12∆ cells (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Trehalose stabilizes membranes in vitro.
source: Intriguingly, prior studies indicate that trehalose stabilizes membranes in vitro and this stabilization may prevent disruptive phase transitions that occur upon rehydration (Crowe et al., 1984, 1987; Erkut et al., 2011; Leslie et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Crowe et al., 1984, 1987; Erkut et al., 2011; Leslie et al., 1994

claim: Hsp12 has been reported to increase membrane stability.
source: Hsp12 also has been reported to increase membrane stability (Sales et al., 2000; Welker et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sales et al., 2000 and Welker et al., 2010

claim: The addition of certain lipids induce the transition of Hsp12 from a disordered state to one with secondary structure.
source: An alternative/additional membrane function for Hsp12 was suggested by the fact the addition of certain lipids induce the transition of Hsp12 from a disordered state to one with secondary structure (Herbert et al., 2012; Singarapu et al., 2011; Welker et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herbert et al., 2012; Singarapu et al., 2011; Welker et al., 2010

claim: Secondary structure prediction and NMR data identify four alpha-helical regions in Hsp12, with each of the three larger helices having the features of an amphipathic helix.
source: Secondary structure prediction and NMR data identify four alpha-helical regions in Hsp12, with each of the three larger helices having the features of an amphipathic helix (Herbert et al., 2012; Singarapu et al., 2011; Welker et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Herbert et al., 2012; Singarapu et al., 2011; Welker et al., 2010

claim: DMPG liposomes incubated in the absence of Hsp12 sedimented into the pellet fraction due to their large size.
source: DMPG liposomes incubated in the absence of Hsp12 sedimented into the pellet fraction due to their large size (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: When incubated in the presence of Hsp12, DMPG appeared in the supernatant fraction.
source: By contrast, when incubated in the presence of Hsp12, DMPG appeared in the supernatant fraction (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Liposome vesiculation mediated by Hsp12 occurred even at low concentrations (Hsp12 - 1.5 μg/ml), with complete vesiculation occurring in a concentration-dependent manner.
source: Liposome vesiculation mediated by Hsp12 was incredibly robust and occurred even at low concentrations (Hsp12 - 1.5 μg/ml), with complete vesiculation occurring in a concentration-dependent manner (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: After the addition of Hsp12, very few intact liposomes were observed, replaced by membrane remnants.
source: After the addition of Hsp12, very few intact liposomes were observed, replaced by membrane remnants (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Trehalose alone did not have any vesiculation activity nor did it inhibit the effect of Hsp12 on liposomes under the conditions tested.
source: Trehalose alone did not have any vesiculation activity nor did it inhibit the effect of Hsp12 on liposomes under the conditions tested (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Hsp12, but not trehalose, exhibits membrane remodeling activity in vitro.
source: These results show that Hsp12, but not trehalose, exhibits membrane remodeling activity in vitro and suggest that their synergistic impact on [GAR+] propagation may result from different biophysical activities.
evidence: Inferred from the liposome vesiculation data

claim: Even when lacking all non-essential hydrophilins, stationary phase yeast cells still demonstrated robust desiccation tolerance.
source: However, even when lacking all non-essential hydrophilins, stationary phase yeast cells still demonstrated robust desiccation tolerance (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Expressing high levels of Stf2 in exponentially-dividing cells did not significantly improve desiccation tolerance and failed to provide any synergistic tolerance with trehalose.
source: Expressing high levels of Stf2 in exponentially-dividing cells did not significantly improve desiccation tolerance and failed to provide any synergistic tolerance with trehalose (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Deletion of Stf2 alone (stf2∆), or in combination with a loss of trehalose synthesis (tps1∆stf2∆) had no effect on the short-term desiccation tolerance of stationary phase yeast.
source: Additionally, deletion of Stf2 alone (stf2∆), or in combination with a loss of trehalose synthesis (tps1∆stf2∆) had no effect on the short-term desiccation tolerance of stationary phase yeast, unlike the pronounced increase in sensitivity displayed by tps1∆hsp12∆ cells (Figures 1A and 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1A and 5B

claim: Unlike Hsp12, Stf2 did not exhibit any detectable secondary structure in the presence or absence of DMPG.
source: Unlike Hsp12, Stf2 also did not exhibit any detectable secondary structure in the presence or absence of DMPG (Figure 5C, Hsp12 + DMPG demonstrates classical alpha-helical CD signature).
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Stf2 fails in vesiculating membranes.
source: Stf2 also fails in vesiculating membranes (Figure 5D–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D–E

claim: Hydrophilins likely carry out distinct biological and molecular functions, despite sharing general physical properties.
source: These functional differences between Hsp12 and Stf2 suggest that hydrophilins likely carry out distinct biological and molecular functions, despite sharing general physical properties.
evidence: Inferred from the functional differences observed between Hsp12 and Stf2

claim: Stationary phase yeast cells lacking both trehalose and Hsp12 (tps1∆hsp12∆) exhibit a greater than 100-fold loss in short-term desiccation tolerance and 10,000-fold loss in long-term desiccation.
source: Here, we demonstrate that stationary phase yeast cells lacking both trehalose and Hsp12 (tps1∆hsp12∆) exhibit a greater than 100-fold loss in short-term desiccation tolerance and 10,000-fold loss in long-term desiccation.

claim: Supplementing cells with only trehalose and Hsp12 was sufficient to make desiccation-sensitive dividing cells desiccation tolerant, with tolerance higher than that which is observed naturally in stationary phase cells.
source: In addition, we show that supplementing cells with only trehalose and Hsp12 was sufficient to make desiccation-sensitive dividing cells desiccation tolerant, this tolerance is higher than that which is observed naturally in stationary phase cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from desiccation tolerance assays

claim: Hsp12 had not previously been implicated in desiccation tolerance.
source: Hsp12 had not previously been implicated in desiccation tolerance.

source: Rather, Hsp12 had been reported to mitigate lethality due to heat stress and osmolarity (Welker et al., 2010).

claim: Desiccation occurs commonly in nature, so the desiccation tolerance conferred by Hsp12 is likely one of its physiological functions.
source: In contrast, desiccation occurs commonly in nature, so the desiccation tolerance conferred by Hsp12 is likely one of its physiological functions.

claim: Hsp12's vesiculation function may play an important role during rehydration.

claim: Hsp12's protective effect may result from aiding in the formation and strength of trehalose in its vitrified state.
